groups.topic: Grill the idea before you build

details.mattpocock: Use it when you already have a plan or idea and want it poked at. Example: you say 'I want a billing page' and it quizzes every branch of that decision.
details.superpowers: Its description says you MUST use it before creating features or changing behavior. Example: 'add a dark mode toggle' triggers it, unless the request is fully specified like 'make the icon cornflower blue'.

details.mattpocock: It does not act until you confirm you both understand the plan. There is no written gate, just that rule.
details.superpowers: Nothing gets built (no code, scaffolding, installs) until you approve the description. Example: it will not create the project folder until you say the design doc is good.

details.mattpocock: Each round it asks every question that can be asked now, then waits for answers, then asks the next batch. Example: round 1 asks 5 settled-prereq questions, your answers unlock round 2.
details.superpowers: It alternates open questions with 200-300 word play-backs, then picks a size and writes it up. Example: after 4 answers it summarizes the audience part and asks what is wrong.

details.mattpocock: You get a numbered batch of questions at once, not one at a time. Example: Q1 to Q5 in one message, each with its own recommended answer.
details.superpowers: Every message ends with exactly one question, kept open and plain. Example: 'Tell me about the last time this annoyed you?' with no list of options.

details.mattpocock: Grilling itself saves nothing; the result is the agreed answers in the chat. Example: you leave with 'yes, use Stripe, no free tier' but no document.
details.superpowers: For a project it writes a document to docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-topic-design.md and commits it. Example: goals, non-goals, constraints, what you decided.

details.mattpocock: When a question needs a fact from your files or tools, it sends a sub-agent to look it up instead of asking you. Example: 'which ORM do we use?' gets looked up, not asked.
details.superpowers: A fresh sub-agent reads the finished design as a stranger builder and lists what it would still need to guess. It then hands off to writing-plans after approval.

details.mattpocock: It scales from one small decision to a whole product because it is just a question loop. Example: grill a one-line API choice in one round.
details.superpowers: It sizes the work: quick task just do it, small change in chat, project gets a doc. Example: 'make the icon blue' skips questions; a new app gets a design doc.

details.mattpocock: Each question carries its suggested answer, worded so a plain 'yes' accepts it. Example: 'Use Postgres? -> Yes, you already run it.'
details.superpowers: It can open a browser tab with visual mockups and offer a throwaway spike build to feel things out. Example: show three layouts side by side before you pick.

best.why: Faster, lighter; recommended answers cut effort

cases.why: Batched questions, recommended answers, no ceremony
Open questions, plain words, mockups
Writes and builder-checks a design doc
First message offers skip
Whole frontier per round

glossary.design tree: A map where each decision leads to the follow-up decisions that depend on it. Example: 'which database' must be settled before 'which migration tool'.
glossary.frontier: The questions you can ask right now because everything they depend on is already settled. Example: once you pick the database, 'which host?' joins the frontier.
glossary.round: One batch of questions sent together, then a wait for your answers. Example: 5 numbered questions, you reply 'yes, yes, no, yes, 3'.
glossary.recommended answer: The agent's own suggested reply written under each question so you can just say yes. Example: 'Q2: Free trial? Recommended: 14 days.'
glossary.sub-agent: A helper AI the main agent spawns for one job and gets a short report from. Example: one helper reads the repo to find the auth library.
glossary.hard gate: A rule that blocks all building until you approve. Example: the agent cannot even run npm install until you say the design is approved.
glossary.design doc: A plain written description of what to build and why, detailed enough that a builder could plan from it. Example: goals, non-goals, constraints.
glossary.play back: The agent retells in its own words what it understood so you can correct it. Example: 'So the app is for freelancers, and invoices must be one click, right?'
glossary.builder check: A fresh sub-agent plays a stranger who must plan from the doc and lists what is still unclear. Example: 'Which payment provider? A wrong guess changes the plan.'
glossary.mockup: A quick visual picture of a screen or layout to react to, shown in a browser tab. Example: three dashboard layouts side by side.
glossary.spike: A fast throwaway build made to learn something, not to keep. Example: a 10-minute hacked page to feel whether the flow works.
glossary.anti-goal: Something that would make the project a failure even if it technically works. Example: 'it works but takes 10 clicks' for a one-click tool.

groups.topic: Turn the idea into a plan

details.pstack: Use it for a large migration or a multi-part change that no narrower skill covers. Example: moving a whole app from REST to GraphQL over several days.
details.mattpocock: You already have a spec or conversation and want it cut into issues. Example: turn a 'user accounts' spec into 6 tickets with blockers.
details.superpowers: You have a spec and need an exact task list before touching code. Example: 'add CSV export' becomes 5 tasks, each with test and commit steps.

details.pstack: You pick how many checks and logs to use based on how risky the work is; it leans high. Example: a one-way database change gets more gates than a copy edit.
details.mattpocock: It will not publish until you approve the breakdown. Example: you say 'merge tickets 3 and 4' and it revises before posting.
details.superpowers: Every step must let the builder write exactly one reasonable thing. Example: 'Run pytest tests/x.py, expect FAIL: function not defined.'

details.pstack: Five phases: frame the goal, design the workflow, run each unit as an experiment, log decisions, verify the whole. Example: one unit = state hypothesis, smallest change, measure, keep or revert.
details.mattpocock: It reads the code, drafts vertical slices, quizzes you on size and blockers, then publishes. Example: it asks 'too coarse or too fine?' before posting.
details.superpowers: It maps files first, writes bite-sized tasks, then checks the plan against the spec itself. Example: self-review catches a function named differently in task 3 and task 7.

details.pstack: It shows the framing and trade-offs once before a multi-hour run, then proceeds. Example: 'here is the rigor level and phase list, go?'
details.mattpocock: It loops on granularity, blocking edges, merge or split until you approve. Example: 'Is ticket 2 really blocked by ticket 1?'
details.superpowers: After saving it asks you to review and choose subagent-driven or inline execution. Example: it recommends one with a one-sentence reason.

details.pstack: You get the designed phase list plus an audit trail a human can read later. Example: a log row per step in the PR.
details.mattpocock: One ticket per slice, each naming the tickets that block it. Example: .scratch/feature/issues/03-login-ui.md, 'Blocked by: 01, 02'.
details.superpowers: A markdown file under docs/superpowers/plans/ with exact paths, signatures and test steps. Example: 'Task 2: Create src/export.py, test tests/test_export.py'.

details.pstack: It runs architect on one-way-door design choices and logs decisions with show-me-your-work. Example: the log is committed so a reviewer reads it.
details.mattpocock: It publishes to whatever tracker was set up, local files or a real issue board. Example: native blocking links on GitHub.
details.superpowers: Its output tells the builder to use one of those two skills. Example: a plan header names subagent-driven-development as the recommended runner.

details.pstack: Built for the ambitious or reviewable-after-you-leave job. Example: start it, step away, return to a trail you can audit.
details.mattpocock: Slices each fit one fresh context so several agents can grab ready ones. Example: ticket 1 and 2 start now, ticket 3 waits.
details.superpowers: If the spec spans several independent subsystems it tells you to write separate plans. Example: auth and billing become two plans.

details.pstack: It sequences work with the scariest unknown first and builds the check before the feature. Example: capture a baseline before the migration.
details.mattpocock: For a rename touching thousands of call sites, it adds the new form, migrates callers in batches, then deletes the old. Example: rename a column in three tickets.
details.superpowers: It lists five likely failure inputs the spec forgot and puts a test for each in the owning task. Example: empty file input for an import feature.

sources.label: mattpocock wayfinder (plans work too big for one session)

best.why: Small parallel tickets; you approve slices

cases.why: Rigor scales, decision log, riskiest first
Blocking edges let agents grab ready work
Exact test-and-commit steps for fresh engineer
Expand-contract keeps CI green per batch
Committed audit trail plus diff

glossary.vertical slice: A thin piece that cuts through every layer (database, API, screen, tests) and works on its own. Example: 'user can log in' end to end, not 'all database tables'.
glossary.tracer bullet: The first thin end-to-end slice used to prove the path works. Example: one button that saves one record through the real stack.
glossary.blocking edge: A link saying ticket B cannot start until ticket A is done. Example: 'Login UI is blocked by Auth API'.
glossary.frontier: The tickets whose blockers are all finished, so they can start now. Example: with tickets 1 and 2 done, ticket 3 joins the frontier.
glossary.expand-contract: A safe way to change something used everywhere: add the new form, move callers over, then delete the old. Example: add column new_name, migrate code, drop old_name.
glossary.wide refactor: One mechanical change that touches thousands of places at once. Example: renaming a shared type used in every file.
glossary.decision log: A written trail of choices and why you made them, so a person can audit later. Example: 'chose Postgres over Mongo because of joins'.
glossary.rigor: How many checks, gates and records the work gets. Example: high rigor means a baseline, a verification script and a log; low means just do it.
glossary.hypothesis loop: Treat each change as an experiment: guess, make smallest change, measure, keep or undo. Example: 'if I batch the writes, load time drops 2x' then measure.
glossary.one-way door: A decision that is hard or impossible to undo. Example: dropping a production table.
glossary.plan file: A markdown file listing exact tasks, files, signatures and test steps for a builder who has not seen the code. Example: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-12-export.md.
glossary.executor: The thing that carries out the plan, either fresh sub-agents per task or one inline session. Example: subagent-driven-development.
glossary.tracker: The place tickets live, like GitHub Issues, Linear, or local files. Example: .scratch/feature/issues/01-setup.md.

details.pstack: Use it when jumping to code would lock in the wrong structure. Example: adding a payments module that touches orders, users and email.
details.mattpocock: Use it while designing or improving a module's interface or deciding where a seam goes. Example: should 'checkout' expose three methods or one?

details.pstack: It needs at least two structurally different candidates before synthesis, even if the first looks fine. Example: one event-based design and one direct-call design.
details.mattpocock: It is a reference of terms and principles, not a procedure; you just apply it. Example: call it 'seam', not 'boundary' or 'service'.

details.pstack: Five phases: map the system, sketch with rival designs, optionally agree, implement against the sketch, scrap if wrong. Example: phase B runs the arena skill for 2+ candidates.
details.mattpocock: Read the glossary and principles, then shape the module with them. Example: check the interface with the deletion test.

details.pstack: By default it goes straight to building; it stops only if you say 'show me before implementing'. Example: '/architect with checkpoint'.
details.mattpocock: In design-it-twice it shows each design, compares them, and gives its own pick. Example: 'design 2 is strongest, borrow design 3's error handling.'

details.pstack: A file of types and signatures with 'not implemented' bodies, plus a rationale with the usage sketch and synthesis decision. Example: createOrder(items): Order with a stub body.
details.mattpocock: It produces a shared language, not an artifact. Example: your team says 'deep module' and 'adapter' the same way every time.

details.pstack: It traces systems with how and why, races candidates in arena, and can attack the result with interrogate. Example: arena returns one synthesized design.
details.mattpocock: The optional DESIGN-IT-TWICE file spawns 3+ sub-agents with different constraints. Example: one minimizes the interface, one maximizes flexibility.

details.pstack: Fits work that spans modules and could set the pattern for the repo. Example: a new service layer.
details.mattpocock: Fits one module, one cluster of shallow modules, or one seam decision. Example: merge three thin wrappers into one deep module.

details.pstack: If the same workaround shows up repeatedly it throws the sketch away and redesigns smaller. Example: casts and 'any' needed everywhere.
details.mattpocock: Imagine deleting the module: if complexity spreads to callers it earned its keep; one adapter is a fake seam, two is real. Example: only add a port if prod and test both vary.

best.why: Forces two real designs before code

cases.why: Two designs, signature sketch, then build
Deletion test shows what to merge
Common terms: seam, depth, adapter
Scrap rule redesigns instead of patching
Design-it-twice spawns 3+ constraint agents

glossary.module: Anything with an interface and an implementation, big or small. Example: a function, a class, or a package.
glossary.interface: Everything a caller must know to use the module, not just the types. Example: method names plus ordering rules, error cases and config.
glossary.seam: A place where you can change behavior without editing that spot; where the interface lives. Example: a payment gateway you can swap for a fake in tests.
glossary.deep module: A lot of behavior behind a small interface. Example: one save() call that handles retries, validation and storage.
glossary.shallow module: An interface almost as complicated as what it does, so it hides little. Example: a wrapper that just forwards every call.
glossary.adapter: A concrete thing that fills a slot at a seam. Example: a Stripe adapter in production, an in-memory adapter in tests.
glossary.deletion test: Imagine deleting the module. If nothing gets harder it was a pass-through; if complexity appears in many callers it was useful. Example: deleting a pure forwarder changes nothing.
glossary.leverage: What callers gain from a deep module: more capability per thing they must learn. Example: one call replaces ten.
glossary.locality: Change and bugs concentrate in one place rather than spreading. Example: fix retry logic once, fixed everywhere.
glossary.signature sketch: Function and type outlines with empty or 'not implemented' bodies, written before the real code. Example: function charge(order): Receipt { throw new Error('not implemented') }.
glossary.arena: A pstack skill that runs several models on the same task and combines their results. Example: four models each propose a design, one synthesis comes back.
glossary.design it twice: Produce at least two very different designs before choosing, because the first idea is rarely best. Example: one callback-based, one queue-based.

details.pstack: Only when you ask for TDD or a regression test, or the bug has an obvious easy test target. Example: a function returns the wrong value and a unit test already exists nearby.
details.mattpocock: When you want to build or fix test-first, or say red-green-refactor. Example: 'build checkout test-first' triggers it.
details.superpowers: It says always: features, bug fixes, refactors, behavior changes. Only throwaway, generated code and config need your OK to skip.

details.pstack: If the test needs broad setup, slow end-to-end, or brittle mocks, skip it and use the closest check. Example: use a repro script instead.
details.mattpocock: Red before green, one slice at a time, tests only at agreed seams. Example: no test at a seam you did not confirm.
details.superpowers: No production code without a failing test first; code written early must be deleted. Example: wrote the function first? delete it, start over.

details.pstack: Write the smallest failing test, run it, quote the failure content to prove it fails for the right reason, fix, rerun. Example: quote 'expected 5, got 0', not just the assertion line.
details.mattpocock: Confirm seams first, then repeat one test, one minimal implementation. Example: seam 'checkout()', first test 'valid cart confirms'.
details.superpowers: Write failing test, watch it fail, minimal code, watch it pass, clean up, repeat. Example: after green, extract duplicate validation while tests stay green.

details.pstack: No human check-in; it reports the failing-before and passing-after evidence at the end. Example: final reply quotes the red output.
details.mattpocock: It writes down seams with a one-line note on what each catches and misses, and waits for you. Example: 'seam: checkout(); catches pricing bugs, misses UI'.
details.superpowers: It asks your human partner only when you want to skip TDD or when stuck. Example: 'config file, skip tests?'

details.pstack: A single focused test that fails before the fix and passes after. Example: test_empty_email_rejected.
details.mattpocock: Behavior tests through the public interface that survive refactors. Example: 'user can checkout with valid cart'.
details.superpowers: Tests plus a verification checklist: every function tested, each watched failing, suite green. Example: unchecked box means you skipped TDD.

details.pstack: Fits one bug with a small obvious test. Example: a wrong default value.
details.mattpocock: Fits a feature built across several vertical slices. Example: checkout built as cart, payment, receipt slices.
details.superpowers: Applies to everything, small or large. Example: a one-line fix still needs a failing test first.

details.pstack: One test, one fix, short report. Skips when a test costs more than the fix.
details.mattpocock: You spend a few minutes agreeing seams before the first test.
details.superpowers: Runs and watches every red and green, and runs the whole project suite before done. Example: bare pytest, not just your file.

details.pstack: Better no test than one that mostly tests mocks or timing. Example: skip a test needing a full browser for a typo fix.
details.mattpocock: Do not write all tests first then all code; one test, one implementation, repeat. Example: no 20 tests before any code.
details.superpowers: If code came before the test, delete it and start from tests. Example: no 'keep as reference'.

best.why: Agreed seams keep tests meaningful, not heavy

cases.why: Cheap test or skip; short report
One slice at a time, agreed seams
Iron law, no exceptions, delete early code
Prefers no test over a bad one
Behavior tests at seams survive refactors

glossary.red-green: Red means a new test fails; green means you wrote just enough code to pass it. Example: red 'expected 15, got undefined', green after adding sum().
glossary.refactor: Clean up code after green without changing behavior. Example: rename variables, remove duplication, tests still pass.
glossary.cheap test: A test you can write quickly with no heavy setup. Example: a unit test calling one function with a literal input.
glossary.regression test: A test that locks in a fixed bug so it cannot quietly return. Example: a test that an empty email is rejected.
glossary.seam: The public boundary where you test and can observe behavior without reaching inside. Example: the checkout() function and its results.
glossary.vertical slice: One thin end-to-end behavior built from one test to one implementation. Example: 'cart total with discount' before 'tax'.
glossary.horizontal slicing: Writing all the tests first, then all the code. It tests imagined behavior and goes out of sync. Example: 20 tests written before any implementation.
glossary.iron law: A rule with no exceptions, named as absolute. Example: no production code without a failing test first.
glossary.tautological test: A test whose expected value is computed the same way as the code, so it can never fail. Example: expect(add(a,b)).toBe(a+b).
glossary.tracer bullet: A first thin slice that proves the path end to end and teaches you what to do next. Example: one test through the real interface.
glossary.mock: A fake stand-in for something external during a test. Example: a fake payment client instead of calling Stripe.
glossary.verification checklist: A list of boxes to tick before calling work done. Example: 'watched each test fail first'.

details.pstack: It is a background principle applied whenever you debug. Example: a crash from a nil value.
details.mattpocock: For broken, throwing, failing, or slow things, or when you say diagnose. Example: a checkout that fails one time in twenty.
details.superpowers: For any test failure, production bug, performance problem, or build failure, especially under time pressure. Example: CI is red and you want a quick patch.

details.pstack: Five short tips, no fixed procedure. Example: reproduce first, never add a guard to silence.
details.mattpocock: A full discipline you may shorten only with a stated reason. Example: skip Minimise only if the bug is already tiny.
details.superpowers: No fixes without root cause investigation first; you must finish each phase before the next. Example: no patch until you have traced the bad value.

details.pstack: Reproduce, keep asking why, then fix every instance of the pattern. Example: grep for the same nil-check bug elsewhere.
details.mattpocock: Build a pass-fail loop first, shrink the repro, rank 3-5 hypotheses, probe, fix with a test, clean up. Example: a 2-second script that fails on this bug.
details.superpowers: Read errors, compare to working code, test one hypothesis at a time, then fix once. Example: log each component boundary to see where data breaks.

details.pstack: The skill lists no check-ins; it just applies the rules while you work.
details.mattpocock: It shows the ranked list before testing and does not block if you are away. Example: you reply 'we deployed #3 yesterday.'
details.superpowers: After three failed fixes it stops and discusses architecture with you. Example: each fix breaks something new.

details.pstack: A fix at the cause, applied everywhere the pattern appears. Example: fix all callers, not one.
details.mattpocock: Failing test at a correct seam if one exists, the cause stated in the commit message. Example: 'Cause: stale cache after restart.'
details.superpowers: A reproduction test first, then a single change. Example: no 'while I'm here' refactors.

details.pstack: It cites no other skills; it is a principle.
details.mattpocock: Reads the glossary and decision records in the area first. Example: use the module names the project already uses.
details.superpowers: Uses test-driven-development for the failing test and verification-before-completion before claiming success. Example: run the test before saying fixed.

details.pstack: Light enough for a quick crash. Example: a one-line null reference.
details.mattpocock: Strongest when the bug is intermittent or a performance regression. Example: raise a 1% flake to a high repro rate.
details.superpowers: Meant for repeat failures and 'just one quick fix' moments. Example: second fix did not work.

details.pstack: A nil check that silences a crash is a symptom fix. Example: fix why it was nil.
details.mattpocock: Every debug log gets a unique prefix like [DEBUG-a4f2] so cleanup is one grep. Example: grep removes them all.
details.superpowers: Three failed fixes signal a wrong design, not a bad hypothesis. Example: shared state causes new symptoms each time.

cases.why: Loop, shrink, ranked hypotheses
Fix root, grep for same pattern
Three fails: question architecture
Baseline measure then bisect
Instrument each component boundary first

glossary.root cause: The real source of the bug, not where it shows up. Example: a bad value created earlier, not the line that crashed.
glossary.symptom fix: A patch that hides the problem without fixing its source. Example: adding a nil check so the crash stops.
glossary.feedback loop: A command you can rerun in seconds that goes red when this bug happens and green once fixed. Example: a script that calls the endpoint and checks the exact wrong output.
glossary.red-capable: Able to fail on this specific bug, not just run without errors. Example: asserts the user's exact symptom.
glossary.tight loop: A feedback loop that is fast, deterministic and sharp. Example: a 2-second test instead of a 5-minute manual click-through.
glossary.minimise: Shrink the repro until every remaining piece is needed to trigger the bug. Example: cut fields from the input until removing any one stops the failure.
glossary.hypothesis: A testable guess about the cause that predicts what happens if you change something. Example: 'if the cache is stale, clearing it fixes it'.
glossary.regression test: A test that locks in a fix so the bug cannot silently return. Example: a test that fails before and passes after.
glossary.seam: The point where code can be tested through its public interface. Example: the function a real caller invokes.
glossary.iron law: A rule stated as absolute with no exceptions. Example: no fixes without root cause investigation first.
glossary.flaky: A bug that only sometimes happens. Example: fails 1 run in 50.
glossary.instrument: Add targeted logging or a debugger probe to see what is happening. Example: log the value entering and leaving each component.
glossary.guard: A check added to prevent an error, such as a nil check. Example: if (x) { ... } added just to stop a crash.

details.pstack: Use it to fan out workers that cover slices or race on one brief. Example: five workers each check a different module.
details.mattpocock: Use it when /to-spec and /to-tickets already produced a spec with tickets. Example: 8 tickets on GitHub with blocking links.
details.superpowers: Use it when you have a plan with mostly independent tasks. Tightly coupled tasks go elsewhere.

details.pstack: Each worker reports PASS, ISSUES or BLOCKED with evidence; missing proof is a gap, not a pass. Example: a worker without the SHA is respawned once.
details.mattpocock: Tickets run in dependency order; code-review comes after all merge. Example: ticket 3 waits on ticket 1.
details.superpowers: Each task gets a spec-and-quality reviewer before the next starts. Example: reviewer rejects, implementer fixes, scoped re-review.

details.pstack: State the done predicate, spawn all workers at once, collect results, return one table. Example: 5 workers, 1 summary.
details.mattpocock: Create integration branch, implementers on ready tickets, merge, repeat as frontier changes, then code-review. Example: ticket 1 merges, which unblocks ticket 3.
details.superpowers: Implementer, task reviewer, up to five fix rounds, then a final branch review. Example: round 4 uses a stronger model.

details.pstack: Parent waits for workers and returns one report; the skill does not ask mid-run.
details.mattpocock: No check-ins; a draft PR opens after the first merge if needed. Example: you see the PR at the end.
details.superpowers: Only irreversible actions, security-sensitive acts, outside side effects, or a hopeless plan stop it. Example: a force-push asks first.

details.pstack: A compact table of results, one-line evidenced issues, and gaps. Example: 4 PASS, 1 ISSUES.
details.mattpocock: The whole spec lands on one branch with tickets resolved. Example: feature/spec-42 ready for review.
details.superpowers: A progress ledger of tasks, rulings, and commits, plus a reviewed branch. Example: 'Task 3: complete'.

details.pstack: Workers are general-purpose agents run in the background, each with its own worktree or output folder.
details.mattpocock: Each implementer calls tdd; the finished branch gets code-review. Example: one implementer fixes all review issues.
details.superpowers: Uses using-git-worktrees at setup and finishing-a-development-branch at the end. Example: starts in an isolated worktree.

details.pstack: All N workers run at once; cost scales with N. Example: 5 workers is about 5x tokens.
details.mattpocock: Ready tickets run in parallel, each in its own worktree. Example: tickets 1 and 2 build at the same time.
details.superpowers: Fresh implementer and reviewer per task; executing-plans does it inline for less. Example: 10 tasks means ~20 agent runs.

details.pstack: Several workers attempt the same job and you pick by first pass, rank all, or best-of. Example: three models try one fix.
details.mattpocock: Each implementer works in its own worktree on its own branch, then a merger agent merges it. Example: no two tickets touch the same checkout.
details.superpowers: After five fix rounds it adjudicates the open findings and moves on. Example: parks non-critical ones in the ledger.

cases.why: Worktree per ticket, merge, then review
Spec and quality review each task
Races same brief, picks by rule
Continuous execution with recorded rulings
Fan out slices, one evidenced report

glossary.sub-agent: A helper AI that the main agent starts for one job and gets a short report from. Example: one implementer per task.
glossary.worktree: A separate checkout of the same repo so work does not collide. Example: each ticket gets its own folder and branch.
glossary.integration branch: One branch where all finished pieces are merged before review. Example: feature/spec-42 collects every ticket's work.
glossary.frontier: The tickets whose blockers are all done, so they can start. Example: tickets 1 and 2 are ready, 3 waits.
glossary.task graph: Tickets connected by 'blocked by' links, not a simple list. Example: ticket 3 depends on 1 and 2.
glossary.fan out: Start many workers at once instead of one by one. Example: five agents each take a slice.
glossary.race: Several workers try the same brief and you pick by a rule. Example: three models fix one bug; you choose the best.
glossary.ledger: A progress file recording done tasks, decisions and commits so work can resume after losing context. Example: 'Task 4: complete'.
glossary.ruling: A decision the agent makes on its own and writes down instead of asking you. Example: 'Ruling: use the spec's wording — plan was wrong.'
glossary.merger subagent: A helper that merges one finished branch into the integration branch. Example: merges ticket 2 after its implementer reports done.
glossary.context pointer: A link to a file, ticket or commit instead of copying its contents into a message. Example: 'read tickets/03.md'.
glossary.spec compliance review: A check that the work matches what the spec asked. Example: reviewer verifies each requirement has a task.
glossary.inline execution: Doing every task yourself in one session instead of sending sub-agents. Example: executing-plans.

details.pstack: Run it when a design is disputed or the stakes are high; the description says "find blind spots" and "tear this apart". Example: before shipping a rewrite of your payment retry code.
details.mattpocock: You name a commit, branch or tag and it reviews everything after it. Example: "review everything since main" before you open a PR.
details.superpowers: It is mandatory after every task in a plan, after a major feature, and before merging to main. Example: you just finished task 2 of 5, so you review before starting task 3.
details.impeccable: It judges how an interface looks and feels, not how the code works. Example: "critique the settings modal" or the homepage URL.

details.pstack: Several different AI models review the same diff, then the lead agent sorts their findings and throws out nitpicks. Example: one model flags a null check, the lead checks the caller and dismisses it.
details.mattpocock: Standards and Spec are judged apart and never merged or reranked. Example: code can pass Standards but fail Spec if it follows every rule yet builds the wrong thing.
details.superpowers: Issues are labelled Critical, Important or Minor, and you must fix Critical and Important before moving on. Example: a missing progress indicator is Important, a magic number is Minor.
details.impeccable: Ten usability checks each get a score from 0 to 4, so the total is out of 40. Example: Error Prevention scores 1, so it lands in the priority list.

details.pstack: Pick the diff, write one paragraph of intent, launch reviewers together, merge findings, then sort them into four buckets. Example: the diff is main...HEAD and the intent is "add retry with backoff".
details.mattpocock: Check the fixed point works, find the spec and the repo's standards, launch two sub-agents together, then show both reports. Example: the spec is issue #45 named in a commit message.
details.superpowers: Grab two commit IDs, fill in a template, send one reviewer, then act on what comes back. Example: base a7981ec, head 3df7661.
details.impeccable: One agent reviews the design and another runs a detector, and neither sees the other until the end. Then the main agent writes the report and asks you questions.

details.pstack: It asks when it cannot tell what the change is supposed to do. It never applies edits on its own. Example: a branch with no commit message or PR text.
details.mattpocock: If you gave no fixed point, or it finds no spec, it asks you. Example: you say "review my branch" and it asks which commit to compare against.
details.superpowers: The skill has no step that asks you anything; the main agent decides what to fix and may push back on the reviewer. Example: reviewer says rename a function, agent shows tests and declines.
details.impeccable: After the report it asks which problem area to fix first and how much to take on. It may skip only when there are fewer than 3 priority issues.

details.pstack: Default panel is Opus, Fable, Sonnet and Haiku, all given the same prompt, so the signal comes from model variety. You can change the list in a settings sheet.
details.mattpocock: One sub-agent checks Standards and one checks Spec, running side by side so neither biases the other.
details.superpowers: One general-purpose sub-agent gets only the commit range and a short description, never your chat history. The template even forbids it from spawning more reviewers.
details.impeccable: A design reviewer and a detector run apart, and a browser inspects the live page when available. Skipping this isolation must be flagged with a DEGRADED banner.

details.pstack: Four model runs plus a lead judgment pass, so it costs and takes the most. (My inference from the step count.) Worth it when a missed bug would hurt.
details.mattpocock: Two sub-agents under 400 words each plus an aggregate step. (My inference.) Fine for every branch.
details.superpowers: One sub-agent and a few git commands. (My inference.) Cheap enough to run after every task.
details.impeccable: Two agents, a code scan, a browser pass, a saved report and a trend check. (My inference.) Only use it for a screen that matters.

details.pstack: A report with Intent, Act On, Consider, Noted, Dismissed and an Agreement Map. It does not change your code. Example: "Act On: unhandled timeout, raised by 3 of 4 models".
details.mattpocock: A Standards section and a Spec section, each kept as written, then one summary line per axis. Example: "Standards: 3 findings. Spec: 1 finding, missing validation".
details.superpowers: Praise first, then issues by severity, then a ready-or-not assessment. Example: "Important: missing progress indicators. Ready to proceed."
details.impeccable: A score table, priority issues and persona red flags in chat, plus a saved copy under .impeccable/critique/. Example: a trend line like 24, 28, 32 out of 40.

details.pstack: A finding raised by two or more models on their own is the highest signal. Example: three models flag the same race condition, so it goes under Act On.
details.mattpocock: Twelve Fowler code smells are always checked, even if the repo has no rules, and the repo's own rules win. Example: it flags Feature Envy as "possible", never as a hard error.
details.superpowers: The reviewer lists what it set aside as out of scope, so nothing disappears silently. Example: "Skipped: DB migration timing, not in the plan".
details.impeccable: It judges look, flow and usability, and a detector flags visual anti-patterns. It will not tell you if your logic is correct.

best.why: Checks code against spec and rules

cases.why: Several models catch blind spots
Spec axis catches wrong or missing features
Cheapest fresh reviewer, SHAs only

glossary.diff: The list of lines that changed between two versions of your code. Example: 12 lines added and 3 removed in retry.ts.
glossary.fixed point: A starting commit, branch or tag you compare against. Example: main, so the review covers everything you did since main.
glossary.spec: The written description of what the change should do, like an issue or a design doc. Example: "Retry 3 times with backoff".
glossary.standards: The repo's written coding rules, such as a CODING_STANDARDS file. Example: "no default exports".
glossary.axis: One separate dimension of judging. Example: Standards is one axis and Spec is another.
glossary.sub-agent: A helper AI the main AI starts for one job, with its own fresh memory. Example: a reviewer that sees only the diff.
glossary.SHA: The unique ID of a git commit. Example: a7981ec.
glossary.lead: The main agent that collects reviewer findings and decides which ones matter.
glossary.intent: One paragraph saying what the change is trying to achieve. Example: "Add retry with backoff to the payment call".
glossary.code smell: A hint that code may be badly shaped, not a proven bug. Example: Duplicated Code means the same logic appears twice.
glossary.severity: How bad a problem is. Example: Critical breaks things now, Minor is a small cleanup.
glossary.heuristic: A rule of thumb for judging usability. Example: "show the user what is happening".
glossary.detector: A script that scans files for known design problems. Example: low-contrast text.
glossary.snapshot: A saved copy of one review run so you can compare later runs. Example: today's 28 out of 40.
glossary.verdict: The final overall judgment. Example: "Ready to merge after two fixes".
glossary.smell: Short for code smell: a hint that code may be badly shaped.
glossary.assessment: One independent review pass. Example: the design review.
glossary.declined to judge: A list of things the reviewer chose not to rule on, with reasons.
glossary.models: Different AI systems, like Opus or Sonnet. Using several catches different mistakes.

groups.topic: Handling review feedback on a PR

details.pstack: A PR is up and you want it pushed to mergeable without re-prompting. Example: CI is red and two reviewers left comments.
details.superpowers: Review comments came in and you must decide what to do before changing code. Example: a reviewer says "remove the legacy path".

details.pstack: It fixes comments it agrees with and replies on judgment calls instead of guessing. It never skips hooks or edits test numbers just to pass.
details.superpowers: Check each suggestion against the real codebase first, and push back with reasons if wrong. No "You're absolutely right!".

details.pstack: Read PR state, fix conflicts then CI then comments, re-check on a timer, stop when green, then report. Example: poll gh pr checks until done.
details.superpowers: Restate the ask, test it against reality, decide, answer, then fix one item at a time. Example: grep shows an endpoint is unused, so propose removing it.

details.pstack: It asks when a fix forces a design choice, before rewriting shared history, and on security or data bot findings. Otherwise it keeps going.
details.superpowers: If any item is unclear it stops and asks before implementing anything. Example: "I understand 1,2,3 and 6; need clarity on 4 and 5".

details.pstack: It uses fix-ci, fix-merge-conflicts and get-pr-comments, the loop timer and the gh command line.
details.superpowers: It stands alone and uses grep, tests and your judgment. Example: it greps for who calls an endpoint.

details.pstack: A green, conflict-free PR plus a report of fixes, deferred comments with reasons, and commit IDs. Example: "Deferred: rename suggestion, unclear target".
details.superpowers: Short factual replies and fixes tested one by one. Example: "Fixed. Build target is 13+, so legacy stays."

details.pstack: It can run a loop with 20 to 30 minute checks and stops after three failed fix rounds (the stop is in the text; the cost is inferred).
details.superpowers: It is a response discipline inside a normal session, not a watcher (inferred).

details.pstack: On a judgment call it leaves the code and replies with what it would have done. It can also triage review-bot comments as fix, dismiss or ask.
details.superpowers: Before building a "proper" feature a reviewer wants, it greps for real usage and offers to delete unused code. Example: nothing calls the metrics endpoint.

cases.why: Fixes CI, conflicts, comments in order
Verify and push back with evidence
Loops on a timer until green
YAGNI grep before building it
Stops and asks before guessing

glossary.CI: Automatic checks that run on every push. Example: tests and lint on GitHub.
glossary.mergeable: Ready to merge: checks pass and there are no conflicts or open comments.
glossary.merge conflict: Two branches changed the same lines and git cannot combine them alone.
glossary.babysit: Keep watching a PR and fixing CI, conflicts and comments until it is ready, so you do not have to.
glossary.YAGNI: "You aren't gonna need it". Do not build things nobody uses.
glossary.triage: Sort issues into fix now, skip or ask.
glossary.judgment call: A decision where reasonable people could disagree, so it needs a human.
glossary.force-push: Overwriting the remote branch history. It can erase others' work.
glossary.hooks: Scripts that run before a commit or push. Example: lint.
glossary.review bot: An automatic reviewer that comments on PRs, like Bugbot.
glossary.performative agreement: Saying "great point!" without checking whether it is true.

groups.topic: Proving it works before saying done

details.pstack: Run it once the work is built and before you say it is finished. Example: you changed a login form and want to confirm it works before reporting back.
details.superpowers: It also triggers before commits, PRs, moving to the next task and handing work to an agent. Example: before writing "tests pass" in a PR description.

details.pstack: Look at the real output, not a stand-in like a cache, a file date or "it compiles". Example: open the running app instead of trusting a build log.
details.superpowers: You may not claim anything works unless you ran the command in this same message. Example: "should pass now" is banned until you run the tests.

details.pstack: Read the real value, then write a script that repeats the same comparison. Example: a script that hits the live URL and checks the response.
details.superpowers: A five-step gate: pick the proving command, run it fully, read all output, check it matches the claim, then speak. Example: run npm test, see 34 of 34 pass, then say it passes.

details.pstack: A deterministic script whose output a reviewer can run again instead of trusting your word. Example: verify.sh that prints PASS or the exact mismatch.
details.superpowers: Every success statement comes with the command result that backs it. Example: "Build passes, exit code 0" with the build line shown.

details.pstack: A red check only counts if the failure is the mismatch you expected, not a crash. Example: quote the real diff "Extra items in the right set", not just the assert line.
details.superpowers: For a regression test, undo the fix, confirm the test fails, then restore the fix. Example: remove your null check and watch the new test go red.

details.pstack: Writing a reusable script takes more effort now but pays back on every rerun (inferred from the text). Keep it local unless the work is large.
details.superpowers: Mostly running the test or build you already have and reading the result (inferred). Fits every small task.

details.pstack: A right answer can come from a broken path, so name the record each fact came from. Example: confirm you read the saved file, not text pasted in chat.
details.superpowers: Words like "should", "probably" and "Great, done!" count as red flags, and the rule covers paraphrases. Example: "looks correct" without a run is a violation.

cases.why: Re-runnable proof on the real artifact
Check diff, not the agent's report
One command, read output, then claim
Script and trail a reviewer reruns
Revert fix, watch fail, restore

glossary.artifact: The real thing you built or changed. Example: the running web page, not the code file.
glossary.proxy: A stand-in that only hints the real thing works. Example: "the build finished" instead of opening the app.
glossary.verification: Proving with evidence that something works. Example: run the tests and read the result.
glossary.claim: Any statement that work is done, fixed or passing. Example: "All tests pass".
glossary.iron law: A rule with no exceptions, even when you are tired or sure.
glossary.exit code: A number a command returns, where 0 means success. Example: build exits 0.
glossary.regression test: A test that stops an old bug from coming back. Example: a test for the crash you just fixed.
glossary.red: A check that fails. Example: a test turns red when the bug is present.
glossary.deterministic: Gives the same result every time you run it.
glossary.pasted output: The actual command result copied into your message as proof.
glossary.script: A small program that repeats a check for you. Example: verify.sh.

groups.topic: Landing the work: PR and branch

details.pstack: The branch has messy commits, a stale description or mixed-up changes. Example: 14 commits named "wip" and "fix".
details.mattpocock: Use it whenever the agent writes a pull request description. Example: you finished a feature and need the PR text.
details.superpowers: Use it when the build is finished and you must choose how to land it. Example: feature complete and you wonder whether to merge or open a PR.

details.pstack: It must show you a plan before rewriting history or force-pushing. Example: "squash 14 commits into 5 in dependency order".
details.mattpocock: Skip preambles and fill three sections only. Example: Summary, Evidence, Merge Danger.
details.superpowers: If tests fail it stops and shows failures; no options appear until the suite is green. Example: 2 failing tests, so no merge offer.

details.pstack: Read the PR, find problems, propose a fix plan, apply it, then confirm the code content did not change. Example: compare git tree hashes before and after.
details.mattpocock: Write a Summary visual, add Before and After evidence, then label the merge risk. Example: a small call tree, a failing then passing test, "one-way door".
details.superpowers: Run tests, check whether you are in a worktree, offer three options, do the pick, then tidy up. Example: pick option 2 to push and open a PR.

details.pstack: Only rewrite when you ask or agree to the plan. Example: it shows the commit grouping and waits for your yes.
details.mattpocock: The template has no questions, so it drafts the body straight away. Example: you get the full PR text in one reply.
details.superpowers: You choose merge, push and PR, or keep as-is, and you must type "discard" to delete. Example: it also asks which base branch if unsure.

details.pstack: Commit order and PR text change but the final code must stay identical. Example: same tree hash before and after the rebase.
details.mattpocock: It only produces PR body text and changes no commits or code.
details.superpowers: It really merges, pushes, deletes the branch and removes the worktree on option 1. Example: git merge then git branch -d.

details.pstack: Tidier commits plus a TL;DR and a guide to the key files. Example: "core logic in src/retry.ts, rest is generated".
details.mattpocock: A Summary with a diagram, Evidence with screenshots or tests, and a Merge Danger rating. Example: "Blast Radius: checkout page".
details.superpowers: One of three finished states for the branch. Example: PR created and the worktree kept for review fixes.

details.pstack: Good for large or noisy PRs, and if still too big it says to split rather than polish. Example: a 900-line PR mixing refactor and feature.
details.mattpocock: Works on tiny and large PRs since it only picks the smallest useful visual. Example: a one-file fix gets a three-line diff sketch.
details.superpowers: The size does not matter; it decides how to land the branch. Example: a one-day feature branch.

details.pstack: It will not hide real behavior changes inside "cleanup". Example: a logic fix must be called out, not squashed silently.
details.mattpocock: Uses diagrams and a one-way or two-way door call. Example: a data deletion is a one-way door.
details.superpowers: It only deletes worktrees it created, and never uses force on its own. Example: leaves a host-owned workspace in place.

glossary.PR: Pull request. A proposal to merge your branch into another branch so others can review it.
glossary.history: The list of commits on a branch. Example: 14 small commits.
glossary.diff: The lines that changed. Example: 120 lines added.
glossary.force-push: Overwriting the remote branch with your rewritten version. It can erase others' work, so it needs care.
glossary.tree hash: A fingerprint of the exact files in a commit. If it matches before and after, the code is the same.
glossary.worktree: An extra folder with its own checked-out branch, so you can work on two branches at once.
glossary.blast radius: How much could break if the change goes wrong. Example: only the settings page, or every customer.
glossary.one-way door: A change you cannot easily undo. Example: deleting production data.
glossary.two-way door: A change you can roll back cheaply. Example: a UI colour tweak.
glossary.template: A fixed form with blank sections to fill in.
glossary.base branch: The branch you plan to merge into. Example: main.
glossary.merge: Combine one branch's commits into another.
glossary.detached HEAD: A git state not on any named branch, often in tool-managed workspaces.

groups.topic: Which skill do I use? (the front door)

details.pstack: Triggered by the word poteto or /poteto-mode, then it picks a playbook for the task. Example: "poteto, fix this bug".
details.mattpocock: You type /ask-matt when you forget which skill to use. Example: "I have a vague idea, where do I start?"
details.superpowers: It loads at the start of any chat and forces a skill check before any reply. Example: even a clarifying question comes after the check.

details.pstack: The reply must name the principles used, and playbook steps are copied into a todo list verbatim.
details.mattpocock: It reads the skill first, then recommends. It never forces a step.
details.superpowers: If a skill might apply even 1%, you must use it. A red-flag table lists excuses to ignore.

details.pstack: Pick a playbook like Bug fix, copy its steps into todos, hand code to sub-agents. Example: Feature playbook starts with the how skill.
details.mattpocock: Open the named skills, then point you to the flow. Example: idea, grill-with-docs, to-spec, implement.
details.superpowers: Look for a matching skill, say "Using X to do Y", then follow it exactly.

details.pstack: It acts on reversible work and pauses only for force-push, deploys, deletions or customer messages.
details.mattpocock: It maps the options and you choose, because the skills it names are typed by hand.
details.superpowers: It does the skill check before clarifying questions, but your direct instructions override it.

details.pstack: It routes to over 20 playbooks plus skills like how, architect and interrogate.
details.mattpocock: It only hints at skills like /tdd and /code-review and cannot start them (model invocation is off).
details.superpowers: It invokes whichever skill fits, such as brainstorming for building or systematic-debugging for bugs.

details.pstack: The agent runs a full playbook end to end, ending in a PR and a short reply.
details.mattpocock: A written route through the skills and when to branch. Example: bugs go to /diagnosing-bugs.
details.superpowers: The agent uses skills as a hard rule, so every task follows a skill.

details.pstack: The main file is about 27KB and it points to more files, so it uses a lot of the agent's memory (my reading of the file size).
details.mattpocock: With model invocation off, nothing loads until you call it.
details.superpowers: The file is about 3KB, but it is read at the start of every conversation.

details.pstack: Each playbook spawns worker sub-agents and reviewers, with fresh agents per round.
details.mattpocock: Only a human can run it, and it also explains when to compact or clear context.
details.superpowers: A table of excuses like "this is just a simple question" tells the agent to check skills anyway.

glossary.router: A skill that tells you which other skill to use. Example: ask-matt says bugs go to diagnosing-bugs.
glossary.playbook: A written step-by-step recipe for one kind of task. Example: the Bug fix playbook.
glossary.flow: A path through several skills in order. Example: idea, spec, tickets, build.
glossary.principle: A short rule about how to work. Example: "prove it works".
glossary.sub-agent: A helper AI started for one job with its own memory.
glossary.verbatim: Word for word, with no changes.
glossary.force-push: Overwriting remote git history. It can erase others' work.
glossary.model invocation: The agent starting a skill on its own. Off means only you can start it.
glossary.context window: The agent's working memory. Long instructions use it up.
glossary.frontier: The set of tasks ready to start now.
glossary.rationalization: An excuse to skip a rule. Example: "it is too simple to need a skill".

groups.topic: Writing skills and agent instruction files

details.mattpocock: Skills, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or any doc an agent reads. Example: shortening your AGENTS.md.
details.superpowers: Whenever you create or change a skill, before you deploy it. Example: adding a new lesson-capture skill.

details.mattpocock: The words in a trigger decide when the agent reads the file, so sharpen them first. Example: lead with the key word.
details.superpowers: You must watch an agent fail without the skill first, even for small edits. Untested text is deleted.

details.mattpocock: No fixed procedure; it gives rules on pointers, layers, goals, key words and pruning.
details.superpowers: Run an agent without the skill, write the skill, test under pressure, then plug excuses. This copies red-green-refactor.

details.mattpocock: Skill-specific advice sits in SKILL-MECHANICS.md. Nothing else is called.
details.superpowers: It requires the test-driven-development skill and runs test sub-agents with pressure scenarios.

details.mattpocock: You read two files and edit with no test runs (inferred).
details.superpowers: Each skill needs baseline and pressure runs with sub-agents (inferred).

details.mattpocock: Every word in an always-on pointer costs on every turn, so prune hard.
details.superpowers: Target is under 150 words for start-up skills and under 500 for others.

details.mattpocock: Rewritten trigger lines and a pruned document. Example: two synonym triggers become one.
details.superpowers: A skill proven against failing runs, with rebuttals to common excuses.

details.mattpocock: Synonyms for one case are collapsed, and it prefers positive wording over bans.
details.superpowers: The description must say when to use it, never summarize the steps, because agents will follow the summary instead.

cases.why: Prunes no-ops and sharpens pointers

glossary.agent doc: Any file an AI agent reads for instructions. Example: AGENTS.md or SKILL.md.
glossary.pointer: Short for context pointer: a line that says when to read a bigger file.
glossary.pressure-test: Test a skill under tempting conditions to see if the agent breaks the rule.
glossary.context pointer: A short line that tells the agent when to read a bigger file.
glossary.skill: A packaged set of instructions an agent can load for one kind of job.
glossary.trigger: The words or situations that make the agent open a file.
glossary.branch: A distinct case a document handles. Example: bug fix versus new feature.
glossary.baseline: What the agent does without your skill, as a starting comparison.
glossary.pressure scenario: A tough test where the agent is tempted to break a rule. Example: deadline plus a tired user.
glossary.red-green-refactor: Write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up.
glossary.sub-agent: A helper AI with its own fresh memory.
glossary.leading word: A short word the model already knows well. Example: "tight" for a fast loop.
glossary.no-op: A line that changes nothing because the agent already behaves that way.
glossary.rationalization: An excuse for skipping a rule.

details.pstack: Run it when you say "reflect" after real work. It skips trivial chats because one-offs are not learnings.
details.mattpocock: You type it yourself after a build that went badly. Example: the agent spent an hour finding the right file.

details.pstack: A synthesizer checks citations, then sorts into Accepted, Rejected or Backlog. It moves anything a lint could enforce to Backlog.
details.mattpocock: A repeatable mistake gets a lint, hook or CI job, not another rule. Only judgment calls become written standards.

details.pstack: Find the transcript, run three reviewers, merge their findings, wait for your OK, then edit skills. Example: a one-line fix to a skill's trigger words.
details.mattpocock: Read the session log, look through seven areas, then show candidates by severity. Example: nothing runs until you choose.

details.pstack: It shows the full Accepted, Rejected and Backlog list and waits, because skill changes affect every future agent. Backlog items file automatically.
details.mattpocock: It only lists suggestions in order of severity and makes no changes itself.

details.pstack: Three reviewers and one synthesizer, plus the plugin-dev skill-development skill for bigger edits.
details.mattpocock: It loads one writing guide first, then works alone without sub-agents.

details.pstack: Concrete edits to existing skills, tuned trigger descriptions or a new skill. Example: tune the description so the skill fires next time.
details.mattpocock: Environment changes like a navigation pointer, a lint, a trimmed AGENTS.md or a new reviewer rule.

details.pstack: Default models are all Opus, and four agents run (cost is my inference).
details.mattpocock: No fan-out in the text, so it should cost little (inferred).

details.pstack: It only keeps lessons likely to repeat. Example: a typo fix is ignored; a missed skill trigger is kept.
details.mattpocock: Coding rules go to the review agent, which has the least load, not the implementer. Example: ban a pattern in review.

glossary.transcript: The saved record of a chat session, every message and tool call.
glossary.retro: Short for retrospective. Look back at what went wrong and how to fix it.
glossary.sub-agent: A helper AI started for one job with its own fresh memory.
glossary.synthesizer: The agent that merges several reviewers' notes into one list.
glossary.backlog: A to-do list for later, not for now.
glossary.navigation pointer: A short line telling the agent where to find something. Example: "API docs are in docs/api".
glossary.guardrail: An automatic check that stops a mistake. Example: a lint rule.
glossary.lint: A tool that scans code for rule breaks.
glossary.AGENTS.md: A file of standing instructions every agent reads in a repo.
glossary.reviewer agent: The agent that checks a diff against the coding standards.
glossary.coding standards: The written rules for how code should look in this repo.
glossary.one-off: A problem that happened once and is unlikely to repeat.
